title: A short interview
lines: Good morning, Mr Lopez. Please sit down. Thank you for coming.
Good morning. Thank you for inviting me.
So, tell me a little about yourself.
Well, I'm twenty-six and I finished my studies two years ago. Since then I have worked in a small electrical company.
And why do you want to work for us?
Your company is bigger, and I want to learn more. I also like that you work with solar energy.
Are you happy to work at weekends sometimes?
Yes, no problem, if I know before.
Very good. We will call you on Friday with our answer.

q.q: What has the man done since he finished his studies?
q.a: He has worked in a small electrical company for two years.

q.q: Why does he want to work for this company?
q.a: Because it is bigger, he wants to learn more, and he likes that they work with solar energy.

q.q: What does he say about working at weekends, and when will they call him?
q.a: He is happy to do it if he knows before; they will call him on Friday.

gaps.s: I also like that you work with ___ energy.
We will call you on ___ with our answer.

title: Tell me about a challenge
lines: Could you give me an example of a problem you had to solve at work?
Sure. Last year, a supplier told us two days before an installation that the panels we had ordered weren't available.
That sounds stressful. What did you do?
First, I called three other suppliers and found one who could deliver similar panels, although they were slightly more expensive.
I called the client straight away, explained the situation and offered to pay the difference ourselves. They were grateful we'd been honest, and the installation finished on time.
And what did you learn from it?
That it's better to communicate bad news early. If I'd waited, the client would have lost confidence in us.

q.q: What problem did the candidate face?
q.a: Two days before an installation, a supplier said the panels they had ordered were not available.
He called three other suppliers and found one who could deliver similar panels, slightly more expensive, and offered to pay the difference.
That it is better to communicate bad news early; waiting would have made the client lose confidence.

gaps.s: The client would have lost ___ in us.

title: Discussing the salary
lines: We'd like to offer you the position. The starting salary would be thirty-eight thousand a year.
Thank you, I'm delighted. I'm very keen on the role. Before accepting, though, could we talk about the salary?
Of course. What did you have in mind?
Based on my experience and on what similar positions pay in the region, I was expecting something closer to forty-two.
I see. I'm afraid our budget for this grade is fairly fixed, but there may be some room elsewhere.
I'd be open to that. What kind of flexibility are you thinking of?
We could review your salary after six months instead of twelve, and add five extra days of training a year.
That's a fair proposal. If the review after six months could be put in writing, I'd be happy to accept.

q.q: How much was offered and how much did the candidate expect?
q.a: Thirty-eight thousand a year was offered; he expected something closer to forty-two thousand.

q.q: Why can't the company simply raise the salary, and what does it offer instead?
q.a: Its budget for that grade is fairly fixed, so it offers a salary review after six months instead of twelve and five extra days of training a year.

q.q: On what condition does the candidate accept?
q.a: That the review after six months is put in writing.

gaps.s: Our budget for this ___ is fairly fixed.

title: The stress interview
lines: I'll be blunt. Your CV is solid, but frankly unremarkable. Why should we choose you over candidates with more experience?

That's a fair challenge. Experience is valuable, but it isn't the same as results. In three years, I've cut design times in my department by a third, which is more than some people achieve in a decade.
You moved jobs after only eighteen months. Isn't that a sign you get bored easily?
I'd put it differently. I left because the company was being restructured and my project was cancelled. I stayed until it was handed over properly, and my former manager would happily confirm that.
Suppose your boss asked you to sign off a design you believed was unsafe. What would you do?
I'd refuse, explain my reasons in writing, and propose an alternative. My signature means something only if I'm prepared to withhold it.
Thank you. I should tell you that this interview was deliberately confrontational. We wanted to see how you handle pressure.
I rather suspected as much. I hope I passed the test.

q.q: How does the candidate answer the claim that his CV is unremarkable?
q.a: He says experience is not the same as results, and points out that he cut design times in his department by a third in three years.

q.q: How does he explain leaving his previous job after eighteen months?
q.a: The company was restructured and his project cancelled; he stayed until it was properly handed over, and his former manager would confirm it.

q.q: What did the interviewer reveal at the end, and how did the candidate react?
q.a: That the interview had been deliberately confrontational to test how he handles pressure; he says he suspected as much.

gaps.s: Your CV is solid, but frankly ___.
My signature means something only if I'm prepared to ___ it.
